unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will learn about the farm. You will name the farm animals and the sounds they make, learn farm words like tractor, barn and field, and talk about the work people do on a farm — feeding, planting and picking. You will see how animals and plants grow: a chick from an egg, a bean from a seed. You will hear a gentle story about helping and working hard. Say the words out loud — this is about speaking with confidence, not perfect spelling.
unit.learningPath:
Begin with the guided teacher launch and learn a few words through pictures and play.
Listen to the Unit story and join in with repeated language.
Complete the twelve language, speaking, early-writing and practical activities.
If you have access to live teacher sessions, meet your teacher three times each week for two weeks for extra practice — these are optional, and every skill in this unit is also fully covered through the teacher launch, story, and speaking and writing activities above.
Finish the ten-question checkpoint, then tell an adult what you can do if one is nearby — or say it out loud to yourself.

readings.title: Amal and the Little Hen
readings.theme: farm animals, sounds, growing and work
readings.setting: Home, online lesson or Grade 1 classroom
readings.passageScript: Amal lived near a small farm. Her grandma kept animals there. Amal loved to visit every morning before the sun grew hot. “Come, Amal,” said Grandma. “There is much work to do on the farm today.” First they went to see the cow. “Good morning, cow!” said Amal. The big brown cow said, “Moo!” Next they saw the sheep and the goat. The sheep said, “Baa!” The goat wanted to eat Amal's hat! Amal laughed and laughed. “Now we must feed the hens,” said Grandma. She gave Amal a small bowl of seed. Amal walked to the barn. The little hen looked hungry. “The hen is hungry,” said Amal. “I will feed her.” She threw the seed on the ground. “Cluck, cluck!” said the happy hen. Then Amal saw something warm in the straw. It was a little white egg! “Grandma, look!” called Amal. “The hen gave us an egg!” “Well done, Amal,” said Grandma. “When you are kind to the animals, they are kind to you.” In the afternoon, they worked in the field. Amal helped to plant a tiny seed in the ground. “Will it grow?” she asked. “Yes,” said Grandma. “With water and sun, the seed will grow into a big bean plant. Everything on a farm grows — the chick grows from an egg, and the bean grows from a seed.” Her big brother Adam drove past on the tractor. “Hard work, little sister!” he called. Amal waved. She was tired, but she was happy. That night, Amal ate warm bread and drank fresh milk from the cow. “I love the farm, Grandma,” she said softly. Grandma smiled. “And the farm loves you, Amal. Good animals need good, kind children like you.”

grammar.title: Name a farm animal
grammar.explanation: Name one farm animal. Say 'a' before most words, but 'an' before a vowel sound: a cow, an ox.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before ox by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an ox, an egg. Say it slowly.
grammar.memoryTip: Open-mouth sound at the start — a, e, i, o, u — means you say 'an'.
grammar.practice: Name three: This is a cow. This is an ox. This is a hen.

grammar.title: Match the animal to its sound
grammar.explanation: Name the animal first, then copy the sound it makes. Make the sound nice and big!
grammar.commonMistake: Children sometimes give only the sound, like 'moo'. Say who makes it in a whole sentence: 'The cow says moo.'
grammar.memoryTip: Say the animal, take a breath, then let the sound out loud.
grammar.practice: Say three animal sounds: The cow says moo. The sheep says baa. The duck says quack.

grammar.title: Say what a farm animal is doing
grammar.explanation: Watch one animal and describe what it is doing now. Add -ing to the action word.
grammar.commonMistake: 'The hen pecking' is missing 'is'. Every 'happening now' sentence needs 'is' before the -ing word.
grammar.memoryTip: Point at the animal, say 'is', then say the busy -ing word.
grammar.practice: Describe three animals: The hen is pecking. The cow is eating. The goat is running.

grammar.title: Describe what an animal has
grammar.explanation: Tell us the parts an animal has, like horns, wings or wool. Say 'It has' and add the part.
grammar.commonMistake: Children often say 'It have wings.' When we talk about one animal we say 'It has wings.'
grammar.memoryTip: Touch that part on your picture or model as you say 'It has'.
grammar.practice: Describe three animals: It has horns. It has wings. It has soft wool.

grammar.title: Put two farm jobs in order
grammar.explanation: Say which farm job happens first, then say what happens next. Order words keep the story clear.
grammar.commonMistake: Sometimes the two steps come out muddled. Ask 'Which one happened first?' before saying the sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: Hold up one finger for 'first' and two fingers for 'then'.
grammar.practice: Say three ordered pairs: First we feed the hens, then we collect the eggs. First we milk the cow, then we clean the shed. First we plant seeds, then we water them.

grammar.title: Spot and name what you see on the farm
grammar.explanation: Name one thing you spot on the farm. Say 'a' before most words, but 'an' before a vowel sound: a barn, an ox.
grammar.commonMistake: Children pop 'a' before ox by mistake. Before an a, e, i, o, u sound we say 'an': an ox, an apple tree.
grammar.memoryTip: Shade your eyes, then listen: open-mouth start — a, e, i, o, u — use 'an'.
grammar.practice: Spot and say three: I can see a barn. I can see an ox. I can see a sheep.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child learns about the farm. They name farm animals and the sounds they make, learn farm words like tractor, barn and field, and talk about what people do on a farm — feeding, planting and picking. They meet the idea that animals and plants grow (a chick from an egg, a bean from a seed), and they hear a gentle story about helping and hard work. The goal is warm, confident spoken English — not perfect spelling.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is a beginner, about 5–7 years old, and is just starting to read. So YOU lead this unit — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, happy sessions of about 15–20 minutes. Lots of pointing, saying, singing, colouring and playing — very little writing.

This guide tells you what to do. The Child Activity Sheet is what your child draws and colours. The Story is one you read aloud.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with a young child
sections.body:
The grown-up holds the device and reads with the child — do not leave a 5-year-old alone with it.

Ask the tutor to make an animal sound slowly so your child can copy it: “Please say the sound a cow makes.”

Ask it to sing “Old MacDonald” with you, or to play an animal-guessing game.

Ask it to give you one more simple farm activity if your child wants to keep going.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching absolute beginners
sections.body:
Keep it short and playful. Stop while it is still fun.

Repeat, repeat, repeat — young children learn by hearing words many times.

Use your hands, face and voice. Moo, cluck, quack and act out the animals!

Praise every try. Confidence matters more than being correct at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Name common farm animals (cow, hen, chick, duck, sheep, goat, horse…).

sections.title: Songs and Rhymes
sections.body:
“Old MacDonald Had a Farm” — sing it together

Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O. / And on that farm he had a cow, E-I-E-I-O. / With a moo moo here and a moo moo there, / Here a moo, there a moo, everywhere a moo moo! / Old MacDonald had a farm, E-I-E-I-O.

Sing a new verse for each animal your child names. Make the animal sound loudly and happily each time — a hen (cluck), a duck (quack), a sheep (baa).

The “Farm Poem” — say it together

Hello to the farmer, / Hello to the tractor, / Hello to the cows in their stall. / Hello to the fields, / Hello to the chicks, / Hello to you all!

Point to each thing (the tractor, the cows, the fields, the chicks) as you say its name.

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over several short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2–3 min)

Greet your child: “Hello! Let's go to the farm today!”

Sing “Old MacDonald” with big animal sounds.

2. Learn the words (5 min)

Point to a farm animal (a picture or a toy) and say the word clearly: “cow”. Ask your child to repeat, then make the sound: “moo”.

Do 4–5 animals at a time. Use big smiles and lots of praise.

3. Play and sing (5 min)

Animal Sounds Game: you make a sound (“Baa!”) and your child names the animal (“sheep!”).

Act It Out: pretend to feed the hens or drive the tractor; your child guesses what you are doing.

4. Story time (5 min)

Read the Story file, “Sagal and the Little Hen”, aloud. Point to the bold words and to any pictures your child has drawn, and ask the simple talk-about questions.

5. Activity sheet (5 min)

Sit with your child and do one or two activities from the Child Activity Sheet. Read each instruction aloud for them.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)

Ask: “What lives on the farm?” Celebrate! Say “Well done!” and one thing they did well.

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
sections.body: Speaking comes before writing. Practise these spoken patterns often:
items: “This is a ______.” (a farm animal)
“The ______ says ______.” (the cow says moo)
“The ______ is ______ing.” (the hen is eating)
“I can see a ______ on the farm.”
“I am ______ing.” (feeding, planting, picking)

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch and tick when your child can do these:
items: Points to and names 5 farm animals.
Makes the sound for 3 animals (moo, cluck, quack).
Names 3 farm things (barn, tractor, egg).
Says what an animal is doing: “The hen is eating.”
Joins in the “Old MacDonald” song.
